name: kuto
why: A reverse JavaScript bundler unpacks minified web apps back into source, a satisfying way of taking something apart.

brief.what_it_is: Kuto is a command-line tool that takes a large ES module JavaScript bundle and splits it into a 'main' file plus a 'corpus' of static chunks. Its output is the main file and the corpus directory, and running it again on a rebuilt bundle reuses existing corpus files where possible and deletes unused ones. It also has a 'kuto info' command that gives basic information about an ES module. Correction to the scout note: Kuto does not unpack minified apps back into source. It splits a bundle, and it works best on output from another bundler.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Kuto makes updating your site's JS smaller by re-using code you've already shipped. The author says the tool started as a way to learn about side-effects through 'kuto info': "This is the origin of the tool; I wanted something that could inform me about side-effects."
brief.how_it_works: Kuto parses the input with acorn and works at the statement level, moving large enough statements into static parts that have no side-effects. Clients can cache those parts forever, and Chromium also caches the bytecode of previously shipped files. Kuto needs the previously generated output to be kept around so the next run can reuse the existing corpus.

commands_seen.context: Run after installing to learn more about the tool (per the README's Usage section).
Splits a JS bundle into a 'main' part and a corpus of code written to out/.
Mentioned inline in the Notes section as giving basic information about an ES Module; no full example given.
Best Practice section: builds Kuto itself by bundling with esbuild, splitting with kuto, then minifying with esbuild.

brief.install_notes: Requires Node 16+. The README says to install via "kuto" and then run npx kuto, without giving an exact install command. esbuild is optional: if it is installed, split and info will transparently compile TS and similar files, but it is not a peerDependency. To get reuse across builds, keep the old generated output in the output dir or point to it with the -c flag, which can be a directory, a local main file, or a URL fetched with fetch().
brief.standout: Kuto moves code-splitting to the end of the build instead of the start. It takes an already-bundled file and reuses previously shipped chunks across deploys, so returning visitors download less. The author describes it as "Think of it as doing code-splitting 'last', rather than first."
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README has no release date, last-commit date, or maintenance note. The only signal is a GitHub Actions Tests badge.
brief.caveats: Kuto works best on large (>1mb) single ESM bundles. The README says an IIFE or webpack output is one giant statement, so it gives little benefit there. Old generated output must be kept, or the -c flag must point to it, or the reuse step does not work. The -d dedup flag is off by default because the README calls it dangerous. The -k flag's author says it 'will probably evolve over time'. The README does not state a license. The scout note's claim that it unpacks minified apps back into source is inaccurate.
quotes: It reduces your download size by re-using code you've already shipped.
Ideally, Kuto operates on a large output bundle from another tool.
Think of it as doing code-splitting 'last', rather than first.
